'''Donna DeEtte Elbert''' (27 January 1928{{snd}}15 January 2019) was an American mathematician and scientist.

== Early life and education ==
Born 27 January 1928 in [[Williams Bay, Wisconsin|Williams Bay]], Wisconsin<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Horn |first1=Susanne |last2=Aurnou |first2=Jonathan M. |date=2022-08-10 |title=The Elbert range of magnetostrophic convection. I. Linear theory |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |language=en |volume=478 |issue=2264 |doi=10.1098/rspa.2022.0313 |issn=1364-5021 |pmc=9364770 |pmid=35966215|bibcode=2022RSPSA.47820313H }}</ref><ref name=":1">“Donna DeEtte Elbert.” Nelson Funeral Homes, 2019.</ref> to William Lawrence Elbert and Sue Melicent Hatch, Donna DeEtte Elbert was the second of three siblings. She attended Williams Bay Elementary School and Williams Bay High School, graduating in 1945.<ref name=":1" />

When Elbert accepted her position to work for astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar in 1948, she did not have any official education in advanced mathematics. It was only after Elbert's employer Chandrasekhar encouraged her to enroll in advanced mathematics courses at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] did she formally obtain education in advanced mathematics such as calculus. Despite her now-formal start in college mathematics, she pursued and graduated with a Bachelors of Fine Arts degree from School of the [[Art Institute of Chicago]] in 1974.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> She also received six weeks of education from [[Parsons School of Design]] in New York City<ref name=":1" /> during the summer of 1956, during which Chandrasekhar worked at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/665139891 |title=A scientific autobiography: S. Chandrasekhar: with selected correspondence |date=2010 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4299-57-2 |location=Singapore; Hackensack, NJ |oclc=665139891}}</ref>

== Science career ==
At 20 years of age and without college education, Elbert began working as a human "[[Computer (occupation)|computer]]"<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Haynes |first=Korey |date=2022-10-27 |title=Donna Elbert's work on planetary magnetic fields finally comes to light |url=https://www.astronomy.com/science/donna-elberts-work-on-planetary-magnetic-fields-finally-comes-to-light/ |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=Astronomy Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> for [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] at the [[Yerkes Observatory]] in Wisconsin in the autumn of 1948.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Ober |first=Holly |date=2022-09-15 |title=Her work helped her boss win the Nobel Prize. Now the spotlight is on her |url=https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/female-math-whiz-predictions-get-credit-in-new-research |access-date=2024-03-16 |website=UCLA |language=en-us}}</ref> She later also worked both at Yerkes and the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Although she originally intended to work under Chandrasekhar only long enough so that she could afford attending design college,<ref name=":0" /> she continued to work for the astrophysicist for over the next thirty years.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

Elbert's first major set of contributions to Chandrasekhar's research, which resulted in her explicit name recognition, was computing solutions to sophisticated differential equations to numerically and algebraically solve for variables in relation to Heisenberg's theory of turbulence.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |date=1949-12-22 |title=On Heisenberg's elementary theory of turbulence |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspa.1949.0156 |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences |language=en |volume=200 |issue=1060 |pages=20–33 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1949.0156 |bibcode=1949RSPSA.200...20C |issn=0080-4630 |last1=Chandrasekhar |first1=S. |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Although she did not gain co-authorship for her mathematical work, Chandrasekhar did give her his thanks in the paper's closing remarks: "In conclusion, I wish to record my indebtedness to Miss Donna Elbert for valuable assistance with the various numerical integrations involved in the preparation of this paper".<ref name=":5" />

After continuing to provide Chandrasekhar with mathematical assistance, he encouraged Elbert, who had no prior official education in advanced mathematics,<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> to study advanced mathematics courses at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin, Madison]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

Elbert achieved co-authorship of 18 papers with Chandrasekhar with her work in analyzing turbulence, [[magnetohydrodynamics]],<ref name=":0" /> polarization of the sunlit sky,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chandrasekhar |first1=S. |last2=Elbert |first2=Donna |date=1951-01-13 |title=Polarization of the Sunlit Sky |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/167051a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=167 |issue=4237 |pages=51–55 |doi=10.1038/167051a0 |bibcode=1951Natur.167...51C |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> rotating flows, convection, and other topics as she progressed into a more central role in Chardrasekhar's group's research, promoting herself beyond her original role as a computer. Despite this step-up, Elbert still conducted much of Chandrasekhar's numerical work, often producing solutions that were more further simplified compared to Chandrasekhar's.<ref name=":0" /> Elbert also authored her own paper, “Bessel and Related Functions Which Occur in Hydromagnetics," published in [[The Astrophysical Journal|''The'' ''Astrophysical Journal'']] in 1957.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Elbert |first=Donna D. |date=1957-08-01 |title=Bessel and Related Functions which Occur in Hydromagnetics. |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1957ApJS....3...77E |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series |volume=3 |pages=77 |doi=10.1086/190033 |bibcode=1957ApJS....3...77E |issn=0067-0049}}</ref>

Elbert continued to conduct research with Chandrasekhar until 1979.<ref name=":4" />

== Elbert range ==
During Elbert's research with Chandrasekhar on the book later published under the title ''Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Stability'',<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Chandrasekhar |first=Subrahmanyan |title=Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Stability |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1961 |isbn=978-0-486-64071-6 |edition=Dover |location=}}</ref> Elbert noted a range of values in the hydrodynamic and hydromagnetic marginal stability curves which result in local minima surrounded by extreme changes.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":6" /> Despite Elbert's key insight and extensive work on the book, she was not given co-authorship of the work by Chandrasekhar. Instead, Chandrasekhar thanked Elbert in only a single footnote.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":6" />

Researcher and scholar Susanne Horn of the [[Coventry University]] (UK) and postdoctoral associate Jonathan Aurnou of [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] (USA) now build on Elbert's key insight about a range of body's specific values on hydrodynamic and hydromagnetic marginal stability curves<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":6" /> that lead to unusually strong magnetic fields in their publication ''The Elbert Range of magnetostrophic convection I. Linear Theory.''<ref name=":0" /> This specific range of values is now known as the Elbert range.<ref name=":4" />

Horn and Arnou reveal that studying the Elbert Range can yield crucial insight into research on objects such as stars and [[exoplanet]]s. In the case of exoplanets, objects that fall within the Elbert Range, such as earth, have substantially strong magnetic fields that can deflect harmful radiation, increasing the probability that life similar to that we know exists on that exoplanet.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" />

=== Very Briefly: The Elbert Range ===
Bodies that have fluid and conductive interiors, such as Earth with its molten liquid metallic core, can create their own magnetic fields due to the movement of charge within their conductive cores. The fluid's motion depends largely on two factors: 1) the combination of the body's rotational velocity and size, which affects the Coriolis Force on the fluids, and 2) convection of the fluid caused by differences in temperature in different sections of the fluid. For bodies that lie in the Elbert Range, the strength of the motion of the conductive fluid caused by the Coriolis Effect and convection are approximately equal, causing the fluid to flow more uniformly in an orderly manner. This uniformity of flow allows for the generation of strong magnetic fields around the body. On the other hand, most bodies do not lie in the Elbert Range, and their conductive cores (if they have one) do not flow in an orderly fashion. Disparate contributions of fluid flow caused by the Coriolis Effect and convection cause disruptive flow patterns, resulting in only weak magnetic fields.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /> Horn and Arnou expanded on Elbert's work regarding the Elbert Range with modern computational and analytical tools.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Despite working long hours for Chandrasekhar, Elbert and her family still remained in close touch with her community in Williams Bay. She served as the treasurer of [[Walworth County, Wisconsin|Walworth County]] Historical Society for 15 years, and her father owned a local barbershop from 1929 to 1970. She picked up many hobbies, including art, piano, and genealogy, because of which she joined the [[Mayflower Society]] and [[Daughters of the American Revolution|Daughters of the Revolution]].<ref name=":1" /> At one point she took piano lessons with Chandrasekhar, though he quit after their teacher progressed through the basics too fast for Chandrasekhar's liking. On vacations, Elbert would read books recommended to her by her boss and discuss them with him upon her return.<ref name=":2" />

Elbert died on 15 January 2019 at the age of 90 at Aurora Lakeland Medical Center in Wisconsin due to a brief illness.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" />
